packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% at 6 months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders picked autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and liquidity-constrained cardholders simply missed more payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up, large administrative dataset.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults raise enrolment therefore they help' logic in a consumer financial product: a choice-architecture nudge changed the nominal enrolment metric without changing the underlying financial outcome, exactly the support team's worry about vanity enrolment.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings
shrouding is a different mechanism than opt-out/opt-in enrolment
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial nudge study showing enrolment-metric movement without behavioural-outcome movement, the core trade-off the brief asks about.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across experiments including a representative 5-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the default is refused, with perceived wealth-manager honesty mediating the effect; framing of the default presentation (asking how much to invest vs. leave safe; accept vs. change) produces smaller but real anchoring effects.
packets.methodology: Multiple experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: it shows a preset default can anchor the chosen amount and that a rejected/individualized default carries a reputational cost, i.e., evidence on exactly the 'helpful vs manipulative default' line that matters for an EU consumer product.
limitations: financial-advice/wealth-management framing rather than a round-up savings feature
outcome is stated risk allocation, not observed behaviour over time
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-decision experiment on default and framing effects on chosen levels and perceived manipulation, squarely on both open design decisions.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Using three natural experiments, default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrolment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default causes substantial losses; variation in active choice tracks transitory attention shocks rather than stable attentiveness.
packets.methodology: Natural-experiment / random-assignment design across three settings, individual-level administrative data.
packets.why_it_matters: Strongest available evidence that default effects can persist and be highly insensitive to outcome quality for individuals choosing for themselves (not via an employer), directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default will 'stick' regardless of fit, and on whether active-choice variation is meaningful signal or noise.
limitations: health-insurance/drug-plan setting, not consumer savings
low-income Medicare population differs from banking-app users
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available individual (non-employer) choice-architecture evidence on persistence and insensitivity of default effects, which the brief needs precisely because it wants defaults studied outside the employer-trust mechanism.
packets.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
packets.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics (job separation, withdrawal on separation, opt-out of auto-escalation) shrink the effect of automatic enrolment and auto-escalation to a steady-state savings-rate increase of only 0.6% and 0.3% of income respectively, with only 40% of auto-escalation defaults sticking at the first escalation date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans, abstract-only for full methods.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrolment gains erode substantially once realistic attrition and opt-out dynamics are modeled, which is exactly the persistence question the brief needs answered before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
no data on a round-up-style consumer product
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrolment durably raises savings amounts, with concrete effect sizes.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: A structural model on 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from complementary deviation and opt-out costs (84% of adherence needs both frictions together), preferences are stable across default changes, and adding an intermediate default tip option would capture 69% of the achievable welfare gain at 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model plus stated-preference survey, large-scale transaction data (8.6M decisions).
packets.why_it_matters: Directly informs the round-up multiplier design: it shows a well-chosen intermediate default level can capture most of the achievable welfare gain, and that default power comes from friction (effort to change) more than preference-shifting, which bears on whether a preset 1x/2x/5x default will anchor people away from their true preference.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
single-transaction choice, no persistence/withdrawal data over months
packets.relevance_reason: Large-scale consumer digital-payment study quantifying exactly how and why preset default levels anchor choices, directly bearing on the multiplier-preset decision.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, social-norm, framing, default-option, and positive-narrative nudges all significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China relative to control, with default options and positive narratives producing the largest backfire effects and impacts varying by income, education, and gender.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing behavioral nudges, including a default option, on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct contradicting evidence against the working assumption that a default lifts enrollment: in this self-directed voluntary-savings RCT the default option actually reduced willingness to contribute, exactly the risk the support team raises, with heterogeneity across demographic groups.
limitations: hypothetical online survey rather than a live financial product
conducted in China, a different cultural/regulatory context than the EU
voluntary pension framing rather than a liquid round-up savings pot
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the shortlist that default options can backfire and reduce contribution willingness.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review/framework synthesising prior default-effect literature, abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a general theory of exactly the persistence question the brief asks (does the effect last at 6-12 months, or is it who-signs-up-not-what-they-do), applicable to a general consumer-behaviour setting rather than tied to pensions.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: The review-level synthesis of downstream default persistence the brief explicitly wants alongside single-study estimates.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: An opt-in payroll short-term (liquid, withdrawable-any-time) savings account at UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate it, but of those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% still received automatic contributions after 12 months.
packets.methodology: Field study of a UK employer payroll savings program, administrative account data over 12 months.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest existing product analog to the round-up feature (short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings) shows opt-in produces very high retention among the self-selected but vanishingly low take-up overall -- the exact trade-off the brief is weighing between opt-in reach and engagement quality.
limitations: delivered through an employer payroll channel, so the 'trusted intermediary' effect the brief says doesn't transfer may inflate retention
not a consumer banking app
packets.relevance_reason: Structurally the nearest product match to the round-up feature (liquid, withdrawable, opt-in savings) despite the employer channel, giving directly comparable take-up/retention numbers.
packets.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
packets.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

packets.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions substantially raised total wealth accumulation, while active-choice tax subsidies induced only 1 cent of extra saving per $1 of subsidy, because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions, while the wealthier 15% of 'active savers' mainly shift assets across accounts.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel analysis of the entire Danish population's savings accounts (41 million observations) comparing responses to active-choice tax subsidies versus automatic employer contributions.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest available causal evidence that defaults change actual saved amounts for the majority who would otherwise not act, while active-choice incentives mostly relabel existing savings — directly bearing on whether the round-up default changes real saving or just nominal enrolment, and on who is helped versus not.
limitations: retirement/tax-subsidized accounts embedded in the Danish welfare/tax system, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
government/employer-mediated contributions rather than a bank round-up feature
no measure of user-perceived manipulation or complaint behavior
packets.relevance_reason: Provides the largest-scale causal estimate distinguishing whether automatic mechanisms change real saved amounts versus active-choice mechanisms merely reshuffling assets — the strongest-evidence answer to the brief's central amount-vs-enrolment question, even though the setting is retirement accounts.
packets.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
packets.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

packets.key_finding: This NBER chapter synthesizes evidence that household financial behavior deviates from classical models across savings, borrowing, payments, and insurance, and reviews how choice architecture, defaults, product design, and disclosure interventions are used to shape these behaviors.
packets.methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter synthesizing empirical household-finance research; abstract-only for specific effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a synthesis-level view across the choice-architecture toolkit (defaults, active choice, product design) the brief is choosing between, serving as the review-level check on effect sizes and trade-offs the brief asked for rather than a single study's estimate.
limitations: broad review chapter, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers mostly the general household-finance literature including many employer-plan studies
abstract gives no specific numbers
packets.relevance_reason: Serves as the review/synthesis of the choice-architecture literature (defaults, active choice, product design) the brief asks for, spanning multiple relevant mechanisms in one place.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

alternates.key_finding: A payment-reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial-management platform cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, measuring fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer financial app can help most users while actively harming a subgroup — exactly the distributional risk the brief flags as a reason not to build something that works only on average; argues for monitoring heterogeneous outcomes (not just aggregate enrolment/savings) before committing to opt-out.
limitations: studies a reminder nudge, not an enrolment default or contribution-level anchor, so C1/C3/C6 questions are untouched
credit card and overdraft fee context rather than round-up savings
Brazilian market, different regulatory and product context than EU banking app
alternates.relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed financial nudge RCT showing clear heterogeneous harm from a nudge, providing the strongest direct evidence for the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk criterion (C5) in a non-employer, non-pension setting.
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Switching exam sign-up to opt-out raised sign-up rates in all cases, but increased actual exam participation/passing only for a single exam among 'responsive' students who had previously engaged with the university; for many exams and 'non-responsive' individuals sign-ups rose with no effect on completion.
alternates.methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out in two study programs.
alternates.why_it_matters: Rigorously demonstrates the support team's disengagement worry: a default can lift nominal sign-up while leaving effortful downstream behavior unchanged for people who weren't going to engage anyway -- precisely the risk of defaulting everyone into the round-up feature without commitment.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product
no data on money withdrawal or complaints, the outcomes the brief cares about
alternates.relevance_reason: The closest available evidence that opt-out defaults raise nominal enrollment without changing effortful engagement, mirroring the brief's central risk trade-off.
alternates.title: Defaults and effortful tasks
alternates.abstract: Abstract Nothing is known about the effectiveness of defaults when moving the target outcomes requires substantial effort. We conduct two field experiments to investigate how defaults fare in such situations: we change the university exam sign-up procedure in two study programs to “opt-out” (a) for a single exam, and (b) for many exams. Both interventions increase task uptake (exam sign-up). Concerning the outcomes which require effort, we find no effects for many exams. For a single exam, the opt-out increases task completion (exam participation) in the study program where the default arguably entails stronger endorsement. Within this program, the effects on successful task completion (exam passing) are heterogeneous: treated students who in the past were willing to communicate with the university (responsive individuals) invest more effort into exam preparation and are more likely to pass the exam than their control counterparts.For non-responsive individuals, we find increased sign-ups but no effects on the target outcomes. Defaults can thus be effective and may be an attractive policy option even when the target outcome requires substantial effort provision. It is, however crucial that the interventions target the appropriate individuals.

alternates.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying GBP170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts capture less than half of consumers' potential savings.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrollment into SMS alerts versus opt-in.
alternates.why_it_matters: Nearly identical setting to the brief's decision -- automatic enrollment into a consumer banking feature at scale -- showing defaults do produce real behavioral savings but capture only part of the potential benefit, calibrating expectations for the round-up feature.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up product
abstract gives no persistence data beyond the experiment window
alternates.relevance_reason: Nearly identical setting (UK bank consumer app automatic enrollment) to the brief's decision, with concrete effect sizes.
alternates.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
alternates.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrolment's boost to participation and contributions, robust at 12 months, is substantially attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings gains though reduced inequality in savings, and a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans and a UK representative panel; structural life-cycle model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Provides the clearest quantified timeline showing default effects fade between 1 and 3 years, which is exactly the horizon the brief asks about for the round-up feature's persistence.
limitations: retirement savings horizon (years) rather than a liquid weeks-to-months savings pot
employer-plan setting
alternates.relevance_reason: Gives explicit 12-month vs 36-month attenuation estimates for the persistence question the brief poses, even though the setting is retirement plans.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show that requiring an active choice (rather than defaulting people in or leaving them to opt in) increases engagement, and an 'enhanced active choice' that highlights losses of the non-preferred option can steer choices while avoiding some ethical concerns of automatic enrollment.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active-choice and enhanced-active-choice interventions against default/no-default conditions, building on Carroll et al. (2009) and the Choi/Laibson/Madrian/Metrick savings literature.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's third onboarding option — forced active choice — against defaults, and proposes a variant that could recover much of the opt-out enrolment lift without passively enrolling disengaged users, exactly the trade-off the brief is trying to resolve.
limitations: field experiments conducted in medication-adherence/health settings, not financial products
does not report savings-specific enrolment or amount outcomes
no long-term (6-12 month) persistence data given in the abstract
alternates.relevance_reason: Introduces and field-tests active choice and enhanced active choice as alternatives to automatic enrollment, the precise mechanism the brief's entry decision is choosing between.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.
